flawed_step: The key step cannot be justified: that a tour T which is not optimal always has an improving tour within ceil(n/2) edge replacements. When |T \ T*| > k, the exchange must be split into intermediate tours, and those intermediates need not exist. With nonnegative weights and no triangle inequality, every tour within distance k of T can be made to cost at least c(T) while a tour further away is cheaper.
counterexample: n=6, k=3 (the same pattern works for all n>=6). T = 1-2-3-4-5-6-1. T* = 1-3-5-6-4-2-1. Weights: edge {6,1} costs 1; the other edges of P_6^2 (edges {i,i+1} and {i,i+2}) cost 0; all remaining edges cost 1. Then c(T)=1 and c(T*)=0. Any tour cheaper than 1 is a Hamiltonian cycle of P_6^2, and that cycle is unique: edges 1-2, 1-3, 6-5, 6-4 are forced; 2-3 would close a triangle, so 2-4; 3-4 would close a 4-cycle, so 3-5. This gives T*. Since |T* \ T| = 4 > 3, no 3-change improves T. So T is a 3-Opt local optimum but not optimal.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. Take T = the path 1..n closed by the edge a={n,1}, and T* = odd cities ascending then even cities descending. Give a cost 1, the other edges of the squared path P_n^2 cost 0, and all other edges cost 1. Every tour cheaper than T is a Hamiltonian cycle of P_n^2. P_n^2 has exactly one such cycle, T*, and it differs from T in n-2 edges. For n>=6, n-2 > ceil(n/2), so T is a ceil(n/2)-Opt local optimum (indeed (n-3)-Opt) but not globally optimal.
